query: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Addition of Cr to high-entropy alloy coatings improves wear resistance across operating temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Solid solution hardening and Laves phase presence for strength
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy coatings without Cr addition
generation.uncertainty: Effect of Cr addition on wear resistance at high temperatures and under different wear conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Wear tests on high-entropy alloy coatings with and without Cr addition at various temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the Cr-added coating is not significantly lower than that of the coating without Cr addition at operating temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: HfMoTaTiZr alloy. Intervention: Addition of 4.2 at% Cr. Processing: Vacuum arc melting. Test conditions: Room temperature. Structure change: Laves phase identified as (Cr, Mo)2(Hf, Ti, Zr) based on EDS and XRD. Property change: Concurrent strength-ductility improvement. Mechanism: Solid solution hardening and Laves phase presence for strength; reticulated structure for ductility. Evidence: measured. Quote: "Together with the analysis results from XRD ( Fig. 1 ) and the conclusion from previous work, [19] it is reasonable to conclude that the Laves phase should be (Cr, Mo) 2 (Hf, Ti, Zr)."
